item.title: Occlusion Myocardial Infarction Missed by ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) Criteria: An Angiographic Emergency Department Cohort
item.description:
Background: The ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)/non-STEMI (NSTEMI) paradigm uses ST-elevation as a surrogate for acute coronary occlusion, but ST-elevation criteria miss many occlusions. The occlusion myocardial infarction (OMI) vs. non-occlusion (NOMI) paradigm classifies patients by the presence of an acute occlusion.

Study objectives: To compare the 2 paradigms in an angiography-selected emergency department (ED) cohort of acute myocardial infarction.

Methods: Retrospective single-center cohort of consecutive adults given an ED diagnosis of STEMI or NSTEMI who underwent coronary angiography between December 2021 and October 2023. OMI was defined as an acute culprit lesion with thrombolysis in myocardial infarction (TIMI) 0 to 2 flow, or culprit stenosis above 70% with a peak emergency department high-sensitivity troponin I above 10,000 ng/L.

Results: Of 1052 patients, 458 (43.5%) were STEMI and 594 (56.5%) NSTEMI; 837 (79.6%) met the study OMI definition. The OMI definition was met by 430 of 594 NSTEMI patients (72.4%), and 430 of 837 OMI patients (51.4%) were STEMI-negative; 51 of 458 STEMI patients (11.1%) had no occlusion. Median peak ED troponin was 155 ng/L in STEMI(+)OMI and 639 ng/L in STEMI(-)OMI (p < 0.001); median ejection fraction was 50% in both (p = 0.004). Angiography within 2 h was performed in 85.7% of STEMI(+)OMI and 15.6% of STEMI(-)OMI patients (p < 0.001).

Conclusion: In this angiography-selected cohort, more than half of the patients who met the study OMI definition were STEMI-negative, and these patients reached angiography far later than STEMI-positive patients with occlusion. Whether such patients can be recognized before angiography requires prospective validation of prespecified electrocardiogram (ECG) criteria.

Korkmaz MS, Çelik K, Danış F

item.title: Temporal Patterns of Sexual Assault Presentations in U.S. Emergency Departments: Implications for Staffing and Forensic Readiness
item.description:
Background: Sexual assault (SA) remains a major public health issue, yet only a fraction of survivors seeks acute medical care in emergency departments (EDs). Although previous studies describe demographic disparities among SA survivors, national patterns of ED arrival timing and their operational implications for emergency care systems remain poorly characterized.

Study objectives: To characterize the demographic and temporal patterns of ED presentations for SA in the United States.

Methods: We conducted a repeated cross-sectional study using the Epic Cosmos database, including U.S. ED encounters related to SA from January 1, 2016 through December 31, 2024. Demographic characteristics and arrival patterns were compared with those of all other ED visits using odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Temporal distributions by day of week and 6-h arrival intervals were analyzed using chi-square testing and standardized Pearson residuals.

Results: Among 391,352,267 ED visits, 245,475 (0.06%) involved SA evaluation. Patients presenting with SA were disproportionately adolescents and young adults, female, Medicaid-insured, and from minoritized racial groups. Overnight arrivals (00:00-05:59) had significantly higher odds of SA presentation (OR, 1.45; 95% CI, 1.43-1.47), with peak presentations occurring on Sundays and Saturdays overnight. Morning presentations were consistently below expected levels. In 2016, 16% of patients presenting with SA arrived by ambulance; by 2024, this number had increased to 18%.

Conclusion: SA presentations revealed distinct demographic and temporal patterns with important operational implications for EDs. Young and socially vulnerable populations are disproportionately affected. The concentration of presentations during overnight weekend hours highlights the need for expanded access to trauma-informed forensic services, including SA Nurse Examiner coverage and prehospital education, especially during high-demand periods.

Pitzele M, Moyer E, Gottlieb M
